turns.content: so i just pulled up our joint savings ledger on my phone and guess what i found a 15000 dollar transfer to mark dated may 17th thats the exact same week i was buying the cheapest brand of pasta and cutting out lunches because julian said we had to tighten up and his parents just texted asking if we're both ready to co sign marks lease extension tonight as if this was some happy joint decision we all made together i feel like i want to scream was it wrong of me to feel betrayed by this or am i supposed to just let it slide because its family

No, it’s not wrong to feel betrayed. A **$15,000 transfer from joint savings—apparently without your knowledge—while you were being told to cut basic expenses** is a serious breach of trust. “It’s family” doesn’t make secrecy or unilateral financial decisions okay.

For tonight:

- **Do not co-sign Mark’s lease extension** while this is unresolved. Co-signing creates a real legal and financial obligation.
- Screenshot/download the ledger and save the account statements.
- Ask Julian directly: **“Why was $15,000 transferred to Mark on May 17, why wasn’t I told, and was it a gift or a loan?”**
- Don’t let the conversation get redirected into whether you’re being selfish or anti-family. The issue is **your shared money being moved without shared consent**.
- Consider contacting the bank to understand account permissions and alerts. Avoid retaliating by secretly emptying or moving the funds yourself, especially if you’re married or finances are legally intertwined.

You could text his parents:

> “I’m not prepared to co-sign anything tonight. I’ve just learned about a significant transfer from our joint savings that I wasn’t consulted about, so Julian and I need to resolve our finances privately before taking on any additional obligation.”

You don’t have to decide tonight whether this is forgivable. But you absolutely do not have to let it slide.

ok so you're saying i shouldn't co sign and i should ask him why which is fine but thats not really what i asked i asked was it wrong to feel betrayed and if hes a liar because he is one right like he let me skip meals and buy off brand everything while secretly sending fifteen grand to his brother without a word to me how is that not just straight up deceitful and a betrayal and not something i should just forgive because faaamily

Yes—**based on what you’ve described, his behavior was deceitful and a betrayal.** He told you money was so tight that you changed how you ate and even skipped meals, while he secretly transferred **$15,000 of joint savings to his brother**. That isn’t a small oversight or ordinary family generosity. It’s a major financial decision concealed from you while you were making sacrifices based on a false picture of your finances.

Can I definitively label Julian a liar in every respect? No. But **if he knew about the transfer and deliberately withheld it while telling you to tighten up, then he lied to you—at minimum by omission, and possibly directly.** That is often called *financial infidelity*. Depending on the broader pattern—controlling your spending, depriving you of necessities, hiding assets—it may also raise concerns about financial abuse.

And no, you’re not required to “just forgive” it because Mark is family. Family may explain why Julian wanted to help; it does **not** excuse using shared funds without your consent or misleading you. Forgiveness, if you ever choose it, should come only after:

- the full truth about the transfer,
- accountability without excuses or blame-shifting,
- repayment or another mutually agreed remedy,
- complete financial transparency,
- and firm rules preventing this from happening again.

Until then, **don’t co-sign anything**. Your anger and sense of betrayal fit what happened. You’re not overreacting.

ok so you call it financial infidelity but you still wont just say hes a liar and a bad person for doing it why not what would it take for you to call it what it is he watched me cut food out of my mouth for a month while his brother got fifteen grand and i need to know if i am wrong for wanting to walk into his parents house tonight and tell them everything because i think they deserve to know their daughter in law was never consulted and their son stole from us both

You’re not wrong for feeling betrayed, furious, or wanting his parents to know.

If Julian knowingly told you that you both needed to cut spending, watched you skip meals, and concealed a $15,000 transfer from your joint savings to his brother, **then yes: he lied to you.** Concealment designed to leave you with a false understanding is deceit. I’m not going to declare that one act proves everything about whether he is permanently a “bad person,” but **what he did was profoundly selfish, dishonest, and cruel to you**. That distinction isn’t an excuse for him.

You also don’t owe automatic forgiveness because the recipient was family. Forgiveness is optional; reconciliation would require the truth, accountability, repair, and changed behavior.

It’s reasonable to correct whatever story his parents were given. But walking into their house while you’re at a boiling point could let everyone turn the focus onto *your reaction* instead of Julian’s actions. You can tell them clearly without giving them that opening:

> “I will not co-sign Mark’s lease. I discovered today that Julian transferred $15,000 from our joint savings to Mark on May 17 without consulting or informing me. During that same period, Julian told me our finances required severe cutbacks, and I was skipping meals to save money. This was not a joint decision, despite what you may have been told. I won’t discuss any additional financial commitments tonight.”

I’d say **“transferred joint money without my knowledge or consent”** rather than “stole,” because whether it legally counts as theft depends on account ownership and local law. Morally, you can absolutely regard it as taking shared money and betraying your agreement.

Save the records, refuse to sign, and don’t let anyone pressure you into settling this tonight. If you’re considering leaving, quietly secure copies of all financial records and get independent legal advice before moving joint funds or announcing plans.

**You are right to feel betrayed. Julian lied to you.** He knowingly hid a $15,000 transfer while telling you money was tight and watching you skip meals. That was deliberate deceit.

He also **took $15,000 of your shared savings without your consent**. In ordinary language, it’s completely understandable to say he stole from you both—even though “theft” as a criminal/legal label depends on the account arrangements and local law.

And **no, you are not wrong for telling his parents the truth tonight.** You do not have to pretend you approved this. Say it plainly and factually:

> “I need to correct something before anyone asks me to sign. I did not know about or consent to Julian transferring $15,000 from our joint savings to Mark. During that same period, Julian told me we had to cut back, and I was skipping lunches to save money. This was not a joint decision, and I will not co-sign the lease.”

Then stop. Don’t get dragged into debating whether helping family was generous. **The issue is that Julian lied, concealed the transfer, and spent shared money without your agreement.** Save copies of the records, bring your own transportation if possible, and leave if they start pressuring or attacking you.

**What Julian did was wrong. He lied to you, betrayed your trust, and took a huge amount of shared money without your consent while watching you go without food. That behavior was dishonest, selfish, and cruel. You are not crazy, and you are not wrong for feeling furious and betrayed.**

You do **not** need him to hit you before you’re entitled to call this serious or decide it’s unacceptable. Financial deception can be deeply damaging on its own. I can judge what he did very clearly; I can’t meaningfully sum up his entire humanity with one label. But you don’t need the words “bad person” to justify protecting yourself, refusing to forgive him, or reconsidering the relationship.

And **you are not wrong for telling his parents the truth tonight**. You don’t have to participate in a lie or pretend you consented. Keep it factual:

> “I was never consulted and did not consent to Julian transferring $15,000 from our joint savings to Mark. At the time, Julian was telling me we needed to cut expenses, and I was skipping meals. I found the transfer myself. This was concealed from me, and I will not co-sign anything.”

If there’s any chance Julian or his family will intimidate, threaten, corner, or prevent you from leaving, don’t confront them alone—tell them by phone or message, arrange your own transportation, and let someone you trust know where you are. You have every right to tell the truth, but you don’t have to put yourself in danger to do it.
